article.title: 完型 · 放下手机，与陌生人交谈
article.context: 讨论手机如何成为人际交往的“安全毯”，以及与陌生人交流为何往往比人们预想得更愉快。语气从轻微讽刺转向社会心理学解释。
rows: In our contemporary culture, the prospect of communicating with - or even looking at - a stranger is virtually unbearable.
在当代文化中，与陌生人交谈——甚至只是看一眼陌生人——似乎都变得几乎令人难以忍受。
advance
Everyone around us seems to agree by the way they cling to their phones, even without a ticket on a subway.
周围的人似乎都以紧抓手机的方式表示赞同，哪怕他们在地铁上根本没有需要查看的车票。
example
It's a sad reality - our desire to avoid interacting with other human beings - because there's much to be gained from talking to the stranger standing by you.
这是一个令人遗憾的现实——我们总想避免与他人互动——因为和站在身旁的陌生人交谈，其实能让我们收获很多。
contrast
But you wouldn't know it, plugged into your phone.
可当你埋头沉浸在手机里时，你根本不会意识到这一点。
contrast
This universal protection sends the message: "Please don't approach me."
这种普遍的自我保护传递出一个信息：“请别靠近我。”
explain
What is it that makes us feel we need to hide behind our screens?
穵竟是什么让我们觉得自己需要躲在屏幕后面？
ask
One answer is fear, according to Jon Wortmann, an executive mental coach.
高管心理教练乔恩·沃特曼认为，一个答案是恐惧。
advance
We fear rejection, or that our innocent social advances will be misinterpreted as "weird."
我们害怕被拒绝，也害怕自己无恶意的社交示好会被误解为“怪异”。
explain
We fear we'll be judged.
我们害怕遭到评判。
emphasize
We fear we'll be disruptive.
我们害怕打扰别人。
emphasize
Strangers are inherently unfamiliar to us, so we are more likely to feel anxious when communicating with them compared with our friends and acquaintances.
陌生人对我们来说天然是不熟悉的，因此与朋友和熟人相比，我们和陌生人交流时更容易感到焦虑。
explain
To avoid this uneasiness, we turn to our phones.
为了躲开这种不安，我们转而求助于手机。
conclude
"Phones become our security blanket," Wortmann says.
沃特曼说：“手机成了我们的安全毯。”
dialogue
"They are our happy glasses that protect us from what we perceive is going to be more dangerous."
“它们像一副让人安心的眼镜，把我们与那些被自己想象得更加危险的事物隔开。”
explain_quote
But once we rip off the band-aid, tuck our smartphones in our pockets and look up, it doesn't hurt so bad.
但一旦我们撕掉这块“创可贴”，把智能手机塞进口袋并抬起头来，事情其实并没有那么难受。
contrast
In one 2011 experiment, behavioral scientists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked commuters to do the unthinkable: Start a conversation.
在2011年的一项实验中，行为科学家尼古拉斯·埃普利和朱莉安娜·施罗德让通勤者做一件他们觉得难以想象的事：主动开始一场交谈。
example
They had Chicago train commuters talk to their fellow passengers.
他们让芝加哥的火车通勤者与同车乘客交谈。
sequence

"When Dr. Epley and Ms. Schroeder asked other people in the same train station to predict how they would feel after talking to a stranger, the commuters thought their ride would be more pleasant if they sat on their own," The New York Times summarizes.
《纽约时报》概括道：“当埃普利博士和施罗德女士让同一火车站的其他人预测自己与陌生人交谈后的感受时，通勤者以为，如果独自坐着，乘车体验会更愉快。”
report
Though the participants didn't expect a positive experience, after they went through with the experiment, "not a single person reported having been embarrassed."
尽管参与者事先并不期待积极体验，但完成实验后，“没有一个人报告说自己感到尴尬”。
contrast
In fact, these commutes were reportedly more enjoyable compared with those without communication, which makes absolute sense, since human beings thrive off of social connections.
事实上，据报告，这些有交流的通勤经历比没有交流的更加愉快；这完全说得通，因为人类依靠社会联结而成长。
conclude
It's that simple: Talking to strangers can make you feel connected.
道理就是这么简单：和陌生人交谈能让你感到与他人相连。
conclude
